question: According to the manual, why is steering sometimes better than braking when there isn't enough room to stop in an emergency?
choice_a: You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
choice_b: Braking always stops a vehicle faster than steering around an obstacle
choice_c: State law requires steering over braking in all emergencies
choice_d: Steering eliminates the need to warn other drivers
explanation: The manual states that stopping is not always the safest action, because you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why does the manual recommend keeping both hands on the steering wheel at all times, not just during emergencies?
choice_a: It is required to keep both mirrors adjusted correctly
choice_b: So you already have a firm grip and can turn quickly if an emergency arises
choice_c: It reduces fuel consumption
choice_d: It keeps the horn within reach at all times
explanation: The manual explains that the best way to have both hands on the wheel in an emergency is to keep them there all the time, since a firm grip is needed to turn quickly.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What should a driver avoid doing while making an emergency turn, since it can cause the wheels to lock and the vehicle to skid?
choice_a: Turning the wheel too slowly
choice_b: Checking mirrors before turning
choice_c: Applying the brake while turning
choice_d: Signaling before the turn
explanation: The manual warns not to apply the brake while turning, because it's very easy to lock the wheels and skid out of control.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What is "counter-steering," as the manual describes it in emergency steering technique?
choice_a: Braking hard immediately after completing a turn
choice_b: Turning the wheel further in the same direction to sharpen the turn
choice_c: Releasing the steering wheel and letting it self-center
choice_d: Turning the wheel back in the other direction once you've passed the obstacle
explanation: Counter-steering means turning the wheel back the other way after passing whatever was in your path; steering and counter-steering should be thought of as one driving action.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: If an oncoming driver has drifted into your lane, which direction does the manual say is usually best to steer?
choice_a: To the right
choice_b: To the left, into the oncoming lane
choice_c: Straight ahead while braking hard
choice_d: It makes no difference which way you steer
explanation: The manual states that if an oncoming driver has drifted into your lane, a move to your right is best, since that driver's natural response will be to return to his or her own lane.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: When leaving the road in an emergency, the manual advises avoiding braking until your speed has dropped to about what point, to prevent skidding on a loose surface?
choice_a: About 40 mph
choice_b: About 20 mph
choice_c: About 5 mph
choice_d: You should never brake after leaving the road
explanation: The manual advises avoiding braking, if possible, until speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then braking very gently to avoid skidding.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.1 - Driving Emergencies (Leaving the Road)

question: What is the correct technique for "controlled braking," per the manual?
choice_a: Apply the brakes fully, then release them the instant the wheels lock
choice_b: Pump the brakes rapidly in short bursts throughout the stop
choice_c: Apply the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements small
choice_d: Apply light, steady pressure regardless of wheel lockup
explanation: With controlled braking, you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements small.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: With the "stab braking" method, what should a driver do after the wheels lock up and the brakes are released?
choice_a: Immediately reapply the brakes before the wheels start rolling
choice_b: Shift into neutral and coast to a stop
choice_c: Pull the parking brake instead of the service brakes
choice_d: Wait until the wheels start rolling again (which can take up to one second), then reapply the brakes fully
explanation: Stab braking releases the brakes when the wheels lock, then reapplies them fully once the wheels start rolling again; reapplying too soon keeps the vehicle from straightening out.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What does the manual warn will happen if a driver "jams on the brakes" during an emergency stop?
choice_a: It will keep the wheels locked up and cause a skid, so the driver cannot control the vehicle
choice_b: It will always stop the vehicle in the shortest possible distance
choice_c: It engages the antilock system automatically on all vehicles
choice_d: It has no effect different from normal braking
explanation: The manual states that jamming on the brakes will only keep the wheels locked up and cause a skid, and if the wheels are skidding you cannot control the vehicle.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.2 - How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What are the two main causes of hydraulic brake failure identified in the manual?
choice_a: Worn tires and an empty fuel tank
choice_b: Loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills
choice_c: Overheated engine and low oil pressure
choice_d: Faulty turn signals and worn windshield wipers
explanation: The manual states most hydraulic brake failures occur for one of two reasons: loss of hydraulic pressure or brake fade on long hills.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure

question: If the brake pedal feels spongy or goes to the floor due to loss of hydraulic pressure, what actions does the manual suggest?
choice_a: Shift into neutral and coast until the vehicle stops on its own
choice_b: Turn off the engine immediately and let the vehicle roll to a stop
choice_c: Downshift, pump the brakes, and use the parking brake, releasing it as needed to control pressure
choice_d: Apply the accelerator to build hydraulic pressure back up
explanation: The manual lists downshifting, pumping the brake pedal, and using the parking brake (while pressing the release button/lever) as ways to slow the vehicle after loss of hydraulic pressure.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure

question: When using the parking/emergency brake to slow a vehicle during hydraulic brake failure, what must the driver also do?
choice_a: Shift into the highest gear available
choice_b: Turn the steering wheel sharply to help slow the vehicle
choice_c: Flash the hazard lights instead of braking
choice_d: Press the release button or pull the release lever at the same time, to adjust brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking
explanation: The manual instructs pressing the release button or pulling the release lever at the same time you use the emergency brake, so you can adjust brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking up.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure

question: On a downgrade, if the brakes fail, what does the manual describe as the driver's "best hope"?
choice_a: An escape ramp, if one is available
choice_b: Shifting into reverse gear
choice_c: Turning off the engine and coasting to a stop
choice_d: Driving into oncoming traffic to find open space
explanation: The manual says your best hope is an escape ramp, and that a driver who loses brakes going downhill should use one if it is available.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure on Downgrades

question: If no escape ramp is available after a brake failure, what does the manual say the driver should do?
choice_a: Take the least hazardous escape route available, such as an open field or side road, as soon as possible
choice_b: Wait as long as possible before leaving the road, to build more speed control
choice_c: Continue down the grade and hope the brakes recover
choice_d: Turn sharply downhill to gain traction
explanation: If no escape ramp is available, the manual says to take the least hazardous escape route, such as an open field or side road, and to make the move as soon as you know the brakes don't work.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.3 - Brake Failure on Downgrades

question: Per the manual, what does a heavy thump or vibration in the vehicle often signal?
choice_a: That the ABS system has activated
choice_b: That the parking brake is engaged
choice_c: That one of the tires has gone flat
choice_d: That the vehicle is due for an oil change
explanation: The manual lists vibration as a major sign of tire failure: if the vehicle thumps or vibrates heavily, it may mean one of the tires has gone flat.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: If the steering feels "heavy" while driving, what does the manual say this is probably a sign of?
choice_a: That one of the rear tires has failed
choice_b: That the vehicle is low on fuel
choice_c: That the ABS malfunction lamp needs replacing
choice_d: That one of the front tires has failed
explanation: The manual states that if the steering feels heavy, it is probably a sign that one of the front tires has failed.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: What is the correct driver response immediately after a tire fails?
choice_a: Hold the steering wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed down
choice_b: Brake hard immediately to stop the vehicle as fast as possible
choice_c: Release the steering wheel to let it self-correct
choice_d: Accelerate briefly to maintain directional stability
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and to stay off the brake, since braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: After stopping following a suspected tire problem, what does the manual say a driver should do?
choice_a: Continue driving unless a warning light appears
choice_b: Get out and check all the tires, even if the vehicle seems to be handling normally
choice_c: Only check the tire on the side the noise came from
choice_d: Call for a tow truck without inspecting further
explanation: The manual says to get out and check all the tires after stopping, even if the vehicle seems to be handling all right, since a failed dual tire may only be noticed by looking at it.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.17.4 - Tire Failure

question: What is the basic function of the Antilock Braking System (ABS), per the manual?
choice_a: It automatically increases the vehicle's overall stopping power
choice_b: It replaces the vehicle's normal braking system
choice_c: It keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications
choice_d: It applies the brakes automatically before the driver reacts
explanation: The manual defines ABS as a computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18 - Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: How does the manual describe ABS in relation to a vehicle's normal brakes?
choice_a: It is a completely separate braking system unrelated to the normal brakes
choice_b: It replaces the normal hydraulic or air brake system entirely
choice_c: It only functions when the normal brakes have failed
choice_d: It is an addition to the normal brakes, not a replacement for them
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to your normal brakes and does not decrease or increase normal braking capability.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18 - Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: When does ABS actually activate, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only when wheels are about to lock up
choice_b: Continuously any time the vehicle is braking
choice_c: Only when the vehicle exceeds 55 mph
choice_d: Only when the parking brake is engaged
explanation: The manual explains that ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up; at all other times the brake system operates normally.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18 - Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: How does the ABS system work mechanically, per the manual?
choice_a: A mechanical valve in the brake pedal limits how hard the driver can press
choice_b: Sensors detect potential wheel lockup, and an electronic control unit (ECU) decreases brake pressure to avoid it
choice_c: The transmission automatically downshifts to reduce speed
choice_d: Air is released from the tires to increase traction
explanation: Sensors detect potential wheel lockup, and the ECU decreases brake pressure to avoid it, adjusting pressure to provide maximum braking without lockup.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.1 - How Antilock Braking Systems Work

question: Under DOT rules cited in the manual, truck tractors with air brakes must have ABS if built on or after which date?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1999
choice_c: March 1, 1997
choice_d: March 1, 2000
explanation: The manual states the Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.2 - Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lbs or more must have ABS if built on or after which date?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: March 1, 2001
choice_d: March 1, 1999
explanation: The manual states hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999 must have ABS.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.2 - Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: When only the tractor has ABS (not the trailer), what benefit does the manual say this still provides?
choice_a: You should be able to maintain steering control, with less chance of jackknifing
choice_b: The trailer will automatically brake in sync with the tractor
choice_c: Overall stopping distance will always be shorter
choice_d: The vehicle can safely exceed normal speed limits in wet weather
explanation: The manual says when only the tractor has ABS, you should be able to maintain steering control and there is less chance of jackknifing, but you should watch the trailer for swinging out.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.5 - ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

question: If only the trailer has ABS and you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, what does the manual say to do?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake as hard as possible
choice_b: Let up on the brakes, if it can be done safely, until you regain control
choice_c: Accelerate to straighten out the combination
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel sharply into the skid direction
explanation: The manual states that when only the trailer has ABS, if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, let up on the brakes (if you can safely do so) until you regain control.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.5 - ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

question: If the ABS malfunction lamp indicates ABS is not working, what does the manual instruct the driver to do?
choice_a: Stop driving the vehicle immediately until ABS is repaired
choice_b: Rely entirely on the parking brake for all stops
choice_c: Drive and brake as you always have, since normal brake functions still work; get the system serviced soon
choice_d: Reduce tire pressure to compensate for reduced braking
explanation: The manual says that without working ABS you still have normal brake functions and should drive and brake as you always have, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.7 - Braking If ABS Is Not Working

question: According to the ABS safety reminders, what kinds of skids will ABS NOT prevent?
choice_a: Brake-induced skids caused by over-braking
choice_b: Skids caused by locked wheels during hard stops
choice_c: Jackknifes caused specifically by over-braking
choice_d: Power or turning skids, caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
explanation: The safety reminders state that ABS won't prevent power or turning skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn, though it should prevent brake-induced skids and jackknifes.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.18.8 - Safety Reminders

question: What four driving errors does the manual identify as causes of skids?
choice_a: Over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast for conditions
choice_b: Under-inflated tires, worn brakes, poor visibility, and low fuel
choice_c: Excessive idling, poor alignment, worn wipers, and low oil
choice_d: Improper cargo securement, bad weather, night driving, and fatigue
explanation: The manual lists over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast for conditions as the four ways a skid can be caused.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19 - Skid Control and Recovery

question: What does the manual describe as by far the most common type of skid?
choice_a: One in which the front wheels lock up from over-braking on dry pavement
choice_b: One in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration
choice_c: One caused by a tire blowout on the trailer
choice_d: One caused by strong crosswinds pushing the trailer sideways
explanation: The manual states that by far the most common skid is one in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.1 - Drive-wheel Skids

question: What can easily stop a drive-wheel skid caused by acceleration on ice or snow, per the manual?
choice_a: Applying the brakes firmly and steadily
choice_b: Downshifting into a lower gear while accelerating
choice_c: Taking your foot off the accelerator (and pushing in the clutch if it's very slippery)
choice_d: Turning the steering wheel sharply away from the skid
explanation: The manual states that skids caused by acceleration, which usually happen on ice or snow, can easily be stopped by taking your foot off the accelerator, pushing in the clutch if it's very slippery.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.1 - Drive-wheel Skids

question: In a bus or straight truck, what happens during a rear-wheel braking skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: The vehicle stops immediately without sliding
choice_b: The front wheels lift off the ground
choice_c: The vehicle accelerates uncontrollably forward
choice_d: The vehicle slides sideways in a "spin out"
explanation: The manual states that in a bus or straight truck, a rear-wheel braking skid causes the vehicle to slide sideways in a "spin out."
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.1 - Drive-wheel Skids

question: With vehicles towing trailers, what can a drive-wheel skid cause, per the manual?
choice_a: The trailer can push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife
choice_b: The trailer disconnects automatically from the tractor
choice_c: The trailer's brakes lock while the tractor's release
choice_d: The combination vehicle accelerates out of the skid safely
explanation: The manual explains that with vehicles towing trailers, a drive-wheel skid can let the trailer push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.1 - Drive-wheel Skids

question: What are the two key steps to correct a drive-wheel braking skid, per the manual?
choice_a: Accelerate hard and turn sharply into the skid
choice_b: Stop braking to let the rear wheels roll again, then counter-steer
choice_c: Apply the parking brake and hold the wheel straight
choice_d: Downshift rapidly and pump the brakes
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to stop braking (to let the rear wheels roll again) and counter-steer as the vehicle turns back on course.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.2 - Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: What mainly causes most front-wheel skids, according to the manual?
choice_a: Worn steering linkage
choice_b: Overinflated front tires
choice_c: Driving too fast for conditions
choice_d: A malfunctioning ABS sensor
explanation: The manual states that driving too fast for conditions causes most front-wheel skids, though lack of tread and improper weight distribution are other causes.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.3 - Front-wheel Skids

question: How does the manual say a driver should stop a front-wheel skid?
choice_a: Turn the wheel more sharply to regain traction
choice_b: Accelerate to shift weight to the rear axle
choice_c: Apply the parking brake immediately
choice_d: Stop turning and/or braking so hard, and slow down as quickly as possible without skidding
explanation: The manual says the only way to stop a front-wheel skid is to let the vehicle slow down: stop turning and/or braking so hard and slow down as quickly as possible without skidding.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.19.3 - Front-wheel Skids

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident scene, per the manual?
choice_a: Protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured
choice_b: Call your dispatcher, photograph the scene, and exchange insurance information
choice_c: Move all vehicles immediately, direct traffic, and file a police report
choice_d: Secure the cargo, inspect the vehicle, and contact the shipper
explanation: The manual states the basic steps at any accident are to protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20 - Accident Procedures

question: If your vehicle is involved in an accident, what should you try to do first to protect the area?
choice_a: Leave it exactly where it stopped until police arrive
choice_b: Get it to the side of the road, to prevent another accident and allow traffic to move
choice_c: Move it to the nearest exit ramp, regardless of distance
choice_d: Turn off all lights so as not to distract other drivers
explanation: The manual says if your vehicle is involved in the accident, try to get it to the side of the road to prevent another accident and allow traffic to move.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20.1 - Protect the Area

question: If you stop to help at someone else's accident, where does the manual say you should park?
choice_a: As close to the wreckage as possible, to block oncoming traffic
choice_b: Directly behind the damaged vehicles
choice_c: Away from the accident, since the area immediately around it is needed for emergency vehicles
choice_d: In the opposing traffic lane to create a barrier
explanation: The manual instructs that if you're stopping to help, park away from the accident, since the area immediately around it will be needed for emergency vehicles.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20.1 - Protect the Area

question: When should you call for assistance if you have a cell phone or CB radio at an accident scene, per the manual?
choice_a: Only after the accident scene has been fully cleared
choice_b: Only if no one else has already called
choice_c: After administering first aid to the injured
choice_d: Before you get out of your vehicle
explanation: The manual says if you have a cell phone or CB, call for assistance before you get out of your vehicle.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20.2 - Notify Authorities

question: When should a severely injured person be moved, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only if the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary
choice_b: As soon as possible, to make them more comfortable
choice_c: Only after emergency services arrive and instruct you to
choice_d: Whenever they request to be moved
explanation: The manual instructs not to move a severely injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20.3 - Care for the Injured

question: How does the manual say a driver should stop heavy bleeding on an injured person?
choice_a: By applying a tourniquet above the wound immediately
choice_b: By applying direct pressure to the wound
choice_c: By elevating the person's head above their heart
choice_d: By washing the wound with water first
explanation: The manual instructs stopping heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.20.3 - Care for the Injured

question: What does the manual identify as causes of tire fires?
choice_a: Overinflated tires and worn brake pads
choice_b: Loose lug nuts and bent rims
choice_c: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
choice_d: Old tread and improper wheel alignment
explanation: The manual lists under-inflated tires and duals that touch as causes of vehicle fires related to tires.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.1 - Causes of Fire

question: What causes electrical system fires, per the manual?
choice_a: Overcharged batteries and worn spark plugs
choice_b: Faulty fuel injectors and clogged filters
choice_c: Excessive idling and worn belts
choice_d: Short circuits due to damaged insulation or loose connections
explanation: The manual attributes electrical system fires to short circuits caused by damaged insulation or loose connections.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.1 - Causes of Fire

question: Where should a driver pull off and park if there is a risk of fire, per the manual's fire-fighting procedures?
choice_a: In an open area, away from buildings, trees, brush, and other vehicles, and never at a service station
choice_b: As close to a service station as possible, for access to water
choice_c: In a parking garage, to shield the vehicle from wind
choice_d: Directly under trees, to provide shade for firefighters
explanation: The manual instructs parking in an open area away from buildings, trees, brush, or other vehicles, and explicitly says not to pull into a service station.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting

question: For an engine fire, what does the manual instruct the driver to do?
choice_a: Immediately open the hood fully to let the fire burn out with maximum airflow
choice_b: Turn off the engine as soon as possible and avoid opening the hood if possible; shoot foam through louvers, radiator, or from underneath
choice_c: Pour water directly into the engine compartment
choice_d: Continue driving to a service station for help
explanation: For an engine fire, the manual says to turn off the engine as soon as you can, avoid opening the hood if possible, and shoot foam through louvers, the radiator, or from underneath.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting

question: For a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, what does the manual say about the doors?
choice_a: Open them fully to let smoke escape
choice_b: Open only the rear door to check on the cargo
choice_c: Keep them shut, since opening them supplies oxygen and can make the fire burn much faster
choice_d: It doesn't matter whether the doors are open or shut
explanation: The manual instructs keeping the doors shut on a van or box trailer cargo fire, especially with hazardous materials, since opening them supplies oxygen and can cause the fire to burn very fast.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting

question: Per the manual's fire chart, what type of fire extinguisher is designed to work on electrical fires and burning liquids?
choice_a: The A:B:C type
choice_b: The Class A type
choice_c: The Class D type
choice_d: The B:C type
explanation: The manual states the B:C type fire extinguisher is designed to work on electrical fires and burning liquids, while A:B:C also covers wood, paper, and cloth.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.21.3 - Fire Fighting / Figures 2.20-2.21

question: Approximately how many deaths per year does the manual attribute to traffic accidents involving drivers who had been drinking?
choice_a: Over 20,000
choice_b: Over 5,000
choice_c: Over 50,000
explanation: The manual states that people who drink alcohol are involved in traffic accidents resulting in over 20,000 deaths every year.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: About how much alcohol can the liver process per hour, according to the manual?
choice_a: About one full ounce per hour
choice_b: About one-third of an ounce per hour, a fixed rate
choice_c: About two ounces per hour
choice_d: About one-half ounce per hour
explanation: The manual states the liver can only process about one-third of an ounce of alcohol per hour, a fixed rate that only time can address.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: What does the manual say will actually sober up a drinker?
choice_a: Drinking black coffee
choice_b: Taking a cold shower
choice_c: Only time — not black coffee or a cold shower
choice_d: Eating a large meal
explanation: The manual explicitly states that only time, not black coffee or a cold shower, will sober a person up, since the liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: What three factors does the manual say determine Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC)?
choice_a: The type of alcohol, the time of day, and your age
choice_b: The amount of food eaten, your gender, and the outside temperature
choice_c: Your driving experience, vehicle type, and road conditions
choice_d: The amount of alcohol consumed, how fast you drink it, and your body weight
explanation: The manual states BAC is determined by the amount of alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, and your body weight.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving

question: Per the manual's BAC effects table (Figure 2.23), a BAC of .08 corresponds to what condition?
choice_a: Definite impairment in coordination and judgment — the "drunk driving limit"
choice_b: A mellow feeling with slight body warmth, and only slightly less inhibited
choice_c: Impaired balance and movement, clearly drunk
choice_d: Loss of consciousness for many people
explanation: According to the manual's BAC effects table, a BAC of .08 shows definite impairment in coordination and judgment and marks the drunk driving limit with criminal penalties.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving / Figure 2.23

question: According to the manual's BAC effects table, at what blood alcohol content do "many" people lose consciousness?
explanation: The manual's BAC table shows that at .30, many people lose consciousness, while at .40 most lose consciousness and some die.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.1 - Alcohol and Driving / Figure 2.23

question: If a driver becomes too ill to operate a vehicle safely, what does the manual instruct?
choice_a: The driver may continue driving if the trip is nearly finished
choice_b: The driver should pull over and wait exactly one hour before resuming
choice_c: The driver must not drive, except in an emergency, when they may drive to the nearest place they can safely stop
choice_d: The driver must immediately hand the vehicle to a passenger, licensed or not
explanation: The manual states that if you become too ill to drive safely you must not drive, but in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.22.3 - Illness

question: What are the three intents of the hazardous materials rules, per the manual?
choice_a: To reduce shipping costs, speed up delivery, and simplify paperwork
choice_b: To limit liability, track inventory, and satisfy insurance requirements
choice_c: To standardize packaging, reduce weight, and improve fuel efficiency
choice_d: To contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment
explanation: The manual states the intent of the hazardous materials rules is to contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
source_note: Utah CDL Manual, Section 2.23.2 - Why Are There Rules?

question: Where must a driver keep shipping papers related to hazardous materials while driving, per the manual?
choice_a: In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach while driving
choice_b: Locked in the glove compartment at all times
choice_c: In the trailer, with the cargo itself
choice_d: Mailed ahead to the delivery destination
explanation: The manual requires hazardous materials shipping papers to be kept in a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.

question: How many identical placards must a placarded vehicle display, and where, per the manual?
choice_a: At least two — on the front and rear only

question: What are hazardous materials identification numbers, per the manual?
choice_a: A two-letter state code followed by three digits

question: What CDL endorsement must a driver have to legally drive a vehicle that requires hazardous materials placards?

question: What tank capacity triggers the requirement for a tank endorsement, regardless of whether the liquid or gas is hazardous?
choice_a: An individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: An individual rated capacity of more than 50 gallons and an aggregate of 500 gallons or more
choice_c: An individual rated capacity of more than 500 gallons, with no aggregate requirement
choice_d: Any tank of any size used to carry liquid cargo
explanation: The manual states a tank endorsement is required for a vehicle designed to transport liquid or gaseous materials in tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.
